photography.intro: Two years photographing a campus in every kind of weather. It is not a side interest that happens to sit next to the engineering — it is where I learned the engineering habits I actually rely on: watch longer than feels necessary, decide what to leave out, and know that the frame is the argument.
photography.outro: A large share of these ran in the University of Dayton Magazine — the same magazine I built the publishing system for.

photographs.title: Corridor
photographs.caption: Backlight doing the composition. Two students, a dog, and a hallway that lines everything up for you if you wait at the right end of it.
photographs.alt: Two students walking away down a sunlit school corridor with a dog beside them, silhouetted against bright windows at the far end

photographs.title: Snowfall
photographs.caption: Falling snow is a depth cue. Shoot it wrong and you get grey; shoot it right and the building sits back three hundred feet.
photographs.alt: University of Dayton campus during heavy snowfall, bare trees and a building fading into white haze

photographs.title: Nest
photographs.caption: Magnolia in full bloom, and a nest in the fork of it. Nobody walking past had seen it. Attention is most of the job.
photographs.alt: A bird's nest resting in the fork of a magnolia branch surrounded by pink blossoms

photographs.title: Fountain
photographs.caption: One frame out of a long burst. The water had to be a shape, not a blur, and he had to still be running.
photographs.alt: A young child in a red shirt running past a fountain, water frozen mid-arc around him

photographs.title: Courtside
photographs.caption: NCAA First Four, 2025. Courtside, arena light, no second attempt at anything.
photographs.alt: A college basketball player driving toward the basket during a packed NCAA tournament game

photographs.title: Lift
photographs.caption: The top of the arc is the only readable moment. You release a fraction before it, because you are not fast enough to react to it.
photographs.alt: Cheerleaders performing a stunt at a basketball game, one flyer inverted at the top of a lift

photographs.title: Afternoon
photographs.caption: Low sun, long grass, someone reading. The quiet frames are the ones the magazine actually used.
photographs.alt: A student lying on sunlit grass reading, warm late-afternoon light across the lawn

paragraphs: I am a web operations and full-stack engineer with a master's in computer science from the University of Dayton. I own websites end to end: building the front end, publishing through the CMS, and keeping the thing healthy once real people are using it.

Most engineers want the build and not the operations. I find the operations more interesting, because that is where you learn what you actually shipped — which pages nobody can find, which release broke a redirect, which template an editor quietly works around every week.

So what I build is mostly leverage. One issue template instead of seven hand-built magazines. One governed publishing path instead of a hundred departments improvising. One precomputed artefact instead of shipping a browser 273,000 rows.

Photography is where that instinct came from, and it is still where I practise it. You cannot include everything; a frame is defined entirely by what you refuse to put in it. Two years of shooting a campus taught me to wait longer than feels comfortable and to accept that a technically perfect frame of the wrong moment is worthless.

What I want next is more of the hard half — production ownership of something large, where the questions are about traffic, reliability and what to do at 2am, not just what the component tree looks like.

playground.intro: Small things, built to understand something. Nothing here is a product.

items.title: Skills readout
items.text: The skills matrix further up. Every entry carries what I use it for and which project it appears in, and all of it is in the HTML — the readout only changes where a pointer user sees it. On a phone, or with JavaScript off, it renders as a plain list with nothing missing.

items.title: This site's build
items.text: No framework and no npm. Content lives in JSON, a 400-line Python generator turns it into flat HTML, and a checker fails the deploy on a dead link, a broken heading outline or a missing alt attribute. Fast because there is nothing in it.

items.title: On-device post forecasting
items.text: Converted a trained engagement model to ONNX and into a CoreML-powered iOS preview app, so a draft post could be scored on-device before publishing rather than round-tripping to a server.

contact.body: A publishing process that keeps breaking. A site nobody can safely deploy. A pile of pages nobody has looked at since 2019. That is the part I want.
contact.availability: Currently open to web operations, website management and full-stack engineering roles — and reading every message myself.
